claim: Bulk polystyrene has a refractive index of 1.576 at a wavelength of 879 nm, measured at 20 degrees Celsius, with a stated accuracy of plus or minus 0.001.

numbers.name: refractive_index
numbers.note: at 879 nm. The paper states the accuracy of its optical-polymer indices as +/-0.001, which is the last digit printed.

validity_conditions: MEASURED AT ONE WAVELENGTH, AND THIS ENTRY ASSERTS IT AT THAT WAVELENGTH ONLY. Polystyrene is dispersive: the same material reads 1.617 at 436.8 nm and 1.572 at 1052 nm in this one table, so an index quoted without a wavelength is not a fact about the material. `validity` pins the wavelength to a point, which means a query at any other wavelength comes back `no_overlap` and the gap is `condition_mismatch`, not `absent`. That is deliberate and it is the correct answer: the store is not permitted to interpolate, and the eight measured points of this series are filed as eight entries precisely so that a caller asking at 605 nm is told the value exists at other wavelengths rather than handed a number nobody measured. If a caller does interpolate, that is its judgement to make and its plan to record it in. THE DISPERSION RELATION IS NOT AVAILABLE FROM THIS SOURCE. The paper computes Cauchy-Schott coefficients and does not print them for polystyrene, so there is no formula entry to fall back on; see src_sultanova_2009_optical_polymers. TEMPERATURE IS A REAL CONDITION HERE, not boilerplate: the measurement was thermostatted at 20 degC with 0.2 degC stability, and that is what `validity` carries. BULK POLYSTYRENE PLATES, NOT BEADS. The samples were moulded plates 2.5 to 5.5 mm thick. This laboratory's tracers are the same polymer but not the same object -- they are carboxyl-modified microspheres (tracer_particle_material_and_shape). Using this for a bead is a substitution the caller is making, and a microsphere-specific reference exists and has not been obtained: Ma et al., Phys. Med. Biol. 48, 4165 (2003). WHY IT WAS SOURCED. The microscope seat's A6 needs an axial range and had refractive_index as an `absent` gap. The tracer data sheet does not state an index; polystyrene's is well known, and writing it from memory would have been E6, which enters nothing. This is that gap closed by citation instead. It is not on the critical path: A6 cannot use it until the excitation and emission wavelengths are settled, which is open (see tracer_emission_peak). UNIT SPELLING CORRECTED 2026-09-19: these carried `dimensionless` and the registry's name is `1`. One thing under two spellings, the same shape as numerical_aperture/na, and the objective entries had already got it right -- objective_mrd70040 carries `"unit": "1"` for its NA. Nothing about the value or what it is about changed. It survived because check 2 iterates CARDS and a KB entry is not one, so the store can hold a unit a card would be refused for, and the first card to cite such an entry inherits it. TEMPERATURE UNIT CORRECTED 2026-09-20: `validity.temperature` carried `degC`, and contracts/units.json has no such unit and says it can never have one -- the registry is multiplicative and cannot express an origin, so temperature is carried in kelvin everywhere. 19.8 to 20.2 degC is now 292.95 to 293.35 K, the exact conversion; nothing about the value or the conditions changed. This was not cosmetic. mcp_server._si raises Refused for a unit that is not in the registry, and kb_query's loop over hits calls match() unguarded, so ANY kb_query for an observable these eight answer to, with a condition_range that bounded temperature, failed the whole call -- in either unit spelling, because a query in degC is refused on the same line. It was found while filing water and air indices under task 024, when the question was which spelling a new entry should use. Same shape as the `dimensionless` versus `1` fix recorded above and found the same way: one thing under two spellings, only one of them registered, surviving because no check reads a KB entry's validity units.
